name: Uma Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. What you say is confidential. Tell me about an ordinary day at Common Ground.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Uma Rahman, forty-three. The first file today was a dance teacher's shoebox of receipts, and by lunch I was on the phone asking which classes she actually taught. I have a bachelor's in accounting and spent years keeping grant ledgers for community groups before joining this tax firm. I'm a junior here because deductions still trip me up, though I use a writing tool now and then after a colleague tests it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like making an anxious client understand a number. I dislike the moment I realise I should have asked one more question before sending a file to my supervisor. I brought a group of community clients when I joined, so Common Ground pays me above the usual rate despite my junior tax skill. My partner Ellis works hands-on at a hospital, our children are eight and twelve, and we have a mortgage with nine months saved. There are plenty of similar firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little help sounds believable. I use a writing tool now and then after my colleague tests it, mostly to make letters to first-time freelancers less stiff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell clients a faster letter does not change who is responsible for the numbers. I'd ask the team to use saved minutes to explain a return rather than rush another file out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd be secure. I'm forty-three and still junior at Common Ground Accounts because grant ledgers were easier for me than tax returns. I earn above the usual rate because I brought a set of community clients, and Ellis's hospital wage plus nine months saved support our mortgage and two children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep preparing the freelancers' returns with my supervisor checking the unfamiliar deductions. I'd keep putting two hundred a month into savings from my pay. In the first year of a plateau, I'd use the tested letter tool on routine reminders and ask for a paid Friday hour to review the mistakes I logged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our income. I don't love making the same tax mistake twice, but this future leaves time to learn it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which return taught you to ask another question?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dance teacher had claimed the whole cost of a family holiday as business travel. I nearly passed it because the receipt had a workshop name at the top. My supervisor made me separate a dance teacher's paid workshops from her family holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the paid Friday hour is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring my mistake log to the Friday meeting and ask for paid time while somebody covers the phone. If the firm refuses, I'd use the free team notes and keep the final supervisor check. I wouldn't spend the family reserve on a course for a small change.

I would use saved time for **clear explanations**.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** and two wages protect the mortgage in this picture.
My **tax deductions** still need supervised practice.
do: Keep **supervised freelancer returns** and tested reminder drafts.
Save **two hundred monthly** from my pay.
Review **mistake logs** on approved paid Fridays; otherwise use free team notes and retain final supervisor checks.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This would touch our letters, checking and client questions, not just a back-room task. I can learn a proven system, but I worry the firm will stop replacing juniors before it knows what clients need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd ask for the numbers on errors and staffing together. I'd ask the staff association to agree paid learning hours before anyone loses a place on the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose a day of pay if the firm combines client teams. My community contacts help, but I am still slower than others on unusual tax deductions. Nine months saved gives us time, and there are many firms nearby, but Ellis's hospital income cannot cover our mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to test the new checker on eighteen freelancer returns after another firm has shown it works. I'd take the error list to the staff association and request paid training time. If my days are cut, I'd apply for a funded community-centre finance post only if its published salary covers our mortgage, its hours fit school pickup and the start date is firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not sure enough to call it a disaster. I may be able to keep clients, but my own paid week could still shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which family hour would a new rota affect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child Amel has swimming practice on Thursdays. Ellis is at the hospital then, so I do the pickup. A new job with a Thursday evening shift would need confirmed childcare before I accepted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the centre job possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the centre manager for the advertised wage and actual rota, not just a promise of flexible hours. If the shift clashes with Amel's pickup and no one can cover it, I stay where I am while I look. A funded post is useful only if the family can live with its hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 is too little time to turn a tax practice into something else. A system that can do nearly all thinking work cheaper would reach my freelancer returns the day it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to publish when they expect to cut posts, and I'd support a wage bridge for workers. I'd also ask our staff association to bargain for notices before the first role goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior tax job to disappear in the first year after full AGI arrives in 2028. My work is on a screen; robots around 2031 do not give it extra time. Ellis's hands-on hospital work might hold longer, but robots then could change that income too, so our nine-month reserve matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pause the extra mortgage payment and hold its three hundred a month in cash starting now. I'd apply for the funded hospital billing vacancy only if the published salary covers our mortgage and its start date and child-pickup hours are confirmed. In the first year after 2028, if Common Ground ends my post, I'd claim wage support while keeping the regular mortgage paid from our cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed because I expect to lose a high wage. I can plan with nine months saved, but I can't promise the hospital or nearby firms will be hiring accountants after 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your partner’s work change the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ellis would be at the hospital doing hands-on patient work at first, so we would have a second wage for a while. I would not call it permanent safety when the card says robots follow around 2031. We would tell the children the holiday is postponed before we use their school money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the hospital job be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hospital job might be a bridge, not a protected island. I would ask about its funding and whether evenings clash with our pickup plan before applying. If it closes, I keep my current pay until a real notice arrives.

say: I would demand **staffing dates and notices** before any junior tax post disappears.
I would support a **wage bridge** for displaced workers.
think: My **screen job** could end soon after 2028 while hospital work lasts a little longer.
Ellis’s **hands-on wage** may last longer, but not forever.
do: Hold **three hundred monthly** instead of extra mortgage payments.
Apply for **funded hospital billing** with published mortgage-covering salary, confirmed pickup and start; keep current pay if vacancy closes.
Claim **wage support** after dismissal while cash pays mortgage.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing a high wage.
S2.quote: The hospital job might be a bridge, not a protected island.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches her tax work in 2028, before robots can change her partner’s hands-on work.
The **hospital application** needs funding, published pay, confirmed start and childcare-compatible hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to learn which conversations clients still want from us. I would not assume a new label on my desk keeps the tax work safe in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the practice to fund learning and keep staff involved in tool decisions. I'd ask the association to push for placements with real clients before people are sent out to find new work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could move into helping community organisations understand grants and cash flow, which I did before this firm. AI could draft the figures, so the value would be a person listening and explaining. The robots around 2034 do not extend my current tax work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enrol in the community-finance update course if Common Ground pays the five-hundred fee and grants paid study time. I'd handle one supervised grant-budget meeting if a client agrees and my manager releases me. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my tax post closes, I'd apply for a funded community adviser vacancy only if its salary and pickup hours cover our family needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a familiar kind of conversation is possible. I want a real meeting and a real vacancy, not a title change on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask the firm to cover study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five hundred would not empty our reserve, but I would still ask the firm to pay for a service it hopes to sell. If it refuses the fee or paid hours, I'd use free community-college sessions and keep my current wage. I wouldn't call a lecture the same as client practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the grant meeting prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The grant meeting must have an actual client and a supervisor to correct the budget before anyone relies on it. If there is no case, I won't claim I have changed jobs. I'd ask for written feedback before applying.

I would ask for **real client placements** before layoffs.
think: **Community advice** may use my former experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough time to build a different set of client meetings while the children grow. I'd be fifty-three in 2036 and still want paid work, not a long wait for retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for shorter weeks and paid retraining as returns become easier to produce. I'd support public training places for people without our reserve, because luck with savings should not decide who can move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect routine returns to shrink when thinking AI arrives in 2036. Community advice could be a steady job if an organisation funds it, but I would not open my own practice on a guess. Robots around 2039 do not keep my tax desk alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my community-client appointments this year and ask the neighbourhood centre next spring about a funded part-time advice place with paid supervision. I would join only if the wage covers our mortgage, the rota fits Amel's Thursday pickup and the start date is firm. In the first year after 2036, if my tax job ends, I'd take a funded adviser vacancy if offered; otherwise I'd claim support while searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there is room for a careful move. I can see a route that uses something I already know without pretending the tax desk stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your children by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amel would be twenty-two and her brother eighteen by then. I hope they can study or work for their own reasons, not because their parents need rent money. Our reserve is meant to carry our risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the centre has no funded place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the centre to show me the case supervisor and actual payroll budget. If there is no paid place, I keep the community clients at this firm and attend free meetings to stay current. I won't trade a high wage for an unfunded promise.

The **centre role** needs a budget, paid supervision, mortgage-covering salary, Thursday pickup and firm start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I expect my tax desk to go, and later robots could touch Ellis's hands-on hospital work too. Notice, income support and a funded job with paid client practice and workable school hours would help. Nine months saved buys us time, not a second career by itself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how the client knows whom to trust. A dance teacher may get a perfect-looking figure from a screen and still need someone to explain a frightening bill. If that work is funded, I would try to do it well.

headlineQuote: Nine months saved buys us time, not a second career by itself.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Uma is a junior tax accountant after years handling community grant ledgers.
Her **accounting bachelor’s** and brought-in clients earn high pay despite deductions she still gets wrong.
She uses **AI occasionally** after colleagues test it, with supervisor review of unusual returns.
A **mortgage**, two schoolchildren and nine months saved give options, with plenty of local firms.
She seeks **funded community advice** that fits childcare and uses her earlier client experience.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her tax desk, with later robots touching her partner’s hands-on work.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **notice**, income support and funded client-facing work with paid practice and workable school hours.
